newsitem.title: FRANCE: EURO-MPS URGE TRANSIT RULES OVERHAUL TO STEM FRAUD.
newsitem.headline: EURO-MPS URGE TRANSIT RULES OVERHAUL TO STEM FRAUD.

text.p: The European Parliament damned the EU's goods transit rules on Thursday, saying they were outdated, too nationally oriented and prone to billions of dollars worth of cigarette and alcohol smuggling.
"Goods cross borders, criminals cross borders, profits from illegal activities cross borders, public authority stops at the borders," said the report, adopted by deputies on Thursday.
"Public authorities continue to see their role as stopping at national borders whilst economic operators, whether legal or illegal, have taken advantage of the new freedoms to full effect," it added.
Euro-MPs called for the transit system's complete overhaul to stem fraud which report author Edward Kellet-Bowman said could total up to 30 billion Ecus ($34 billion) a year.

European Union transit rules allow freight to cross the bloc's 15 countries and several neighbouring states tax free, with customs duties, value-added tax and excise duties payable only at the goods' final, third-country destinations.
But some operators fake transit papers and offload on to the EU market cigarettes, alcohol and other high value items, which never make it to declared destinations where taxes would be due.
The parliament's inquiry, which started in December 1995, was the first under new investigative powers granted to Euro-MPs by the 1992 Maastricht Treaty.

It revealed a gaping contradiction between the EU's decision in 1993 to abolish internal barriers to the circulation of goods and its failure to update an archaic, paper-based customs system to deal with the change.
The result, it said, has been vast profits for criminals at the expense of the EU's budget, national coffers and the private companies which post guarantees for transit operations.

Parliament demanded a string of reforms to the system, designed in the 1960s for a European Community of only six members but now handling 18 million operations a year in the EU, Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Norway, Iceland, Poland, Hungary, the Czech Republic and Slovakia -- its neighbours in the European Free Trade Association and the Visegrad grouping.

It said the outdated and fragmented customs system, which used rubber stamps which could be stolen or falsified, should be replaced by a computerised network for which the EU has already promised 50 percent of the money.
Parliament said access to the transit system should be limited, particularly for goods like alcohol and cigarettes.
It urged the committee of the 23 participating European countries to conduct a thorough investigation into cigarette trade and to recommend sanctions against fraudsters.
Parliament's inquiry said cigarette smuggling accounted for 19 percent of fraud and a massive 47 percent of lost tax money.
Members of parliament said revamped customs codes should permit spot checks on lorries anywhere on EU territory and a coordinated system of physical checks at land borders and ports.

They also demanded better cooperation between national prosecutors and said the European Commission's anti-fraud unit (UCLAF) should have the same powers as national authorities to initiate criminal proceedings.
It was also vital, they said, to get better cooperation from neighbouring countries like Switzerland, where banking secrecy laws played into fraudsters' hands.

John Tomlinson, a British Socialist member of the parliament, told a recent news conference that one quarter of all transit lorries passed through Switzerland and cited examples of American cigarettes arriving in the Belgian port of Antwerp destined for Azerbaijan. ($=.88 European currency unit)
